title: babykev.docs
text:
babykev docs list every module, class, method and function, one line each babykev docs module NAME one module: a heading per symbol, its signature, docstring and table babykev docs check count what is typed and documented, list every gap, fail if any
Types come from the annotations, the description of a parameter from its docment (the comment beside it, read by fastcore) and the summary from the docstring. Nothing is written twice. The output is plain Markdown with no links, ids or URLs, so that a person, an agent or the docs site can read it. list and module show the package; check holds the package, the tests, and the Python files at the root and under docs/ to the convention.
How to write a docment, so that the formatter and the linter leave it alone: one parameter per line, a trailing comma after the last, the comment two spaces after the code; the return’s comment after the colon of the def line. Every function in this file is an example. The whole line must fit in 100 characters: the formatter wraps a longer line, the comment lands away from its parameter, and check reports it as missing. The formatter never joins a line that carries a comment, and no lint rule looks inside one.

title: The mask
text:
A request asks several questions about one context. The model reads the context once and answers every question in the same pass, and yet no question can influence another. What makes that possible is the attention mask, built by branch_mask.
This page is a notebook. The reference entry below is pulled from the source, and the grids are what the code printed when the notebook was last run.
def branch_mask(
    seg:list[int], # The segment of each token: 0 for the state, k for question k
    device:str, # Where to build the mask
    dtype:torch.dtype=torch.float32, # The number type of the model's attention scores
)->torch.Tensor: # Shape [1, 1, n, n]: 0 where i may attend to j, very negative elsewhere
Build the block-causal mask: a token sees the state and its own question, never a sibling.
Token i may attend to token j when j is not after i, and j is in the state or in the same question as i. The mask is added to the attention scores, so a blocked pair gets the most negative number the type can hold.

title: The mask
text:
A small request
Take three context tokens, then two questions of two tokens each. encode gives every token a segment: 0 for the context, 1 for the first question, 2 for the second. In the grid, each row is a token, and a filled cell means it may attend to the token in that column.

def show(seg, mask=branch_mask):
    allow = mask(seg, "cpu")[0, 0] == 0
    print("   " + " ".join(str(s) for s in seg))
    for s, row in zip(seg, allow, strict=True):
        print(f"{s}  " + " ".join("#" if ok else "." for ok in row))


show([0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 2, 2])

   0 0 0 1 1 2 2
0  # . . . . . .
0  # # . . . . .
0  # # # . . . .
1  # # # # . . .
1  # # # # # . .
2  # # # . . # .
2  # # # . . # #


Read the last two rows. The second question sees the three context tokens and itself. The two columns of the first question are empty: to the second question, the first one is not there.

title: The mask
text:
The rule
Token i may attend to token j when j is not later than i, and j is in the context or in the same question as i. Nothing else. A longer request shows the same blocks:

show([0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 2, 3, 3])

   0 0 1 1 1 2 3 3
0  # . . . . . . .
0  # # . . . . . .
1  # # # . . . . .
1  # # # # . . . .
1  # # # # # . . .
2  # # . . . # . .
3  # # . . . . # .
3  # # . . . . # #

title: The mask
section: The mask as it was at step 05
text:
The mask as it was at step 05
The model arrived with a plain causal mask, the usual one for a language model: every token sees everything before it. Here is the same request under that mask. The second question’s rows now have the first question’s columns filled: it reads the first question as if it were part of the context. Nothing crashes, the model still returns probabilities, and the answers to one question depend on which questions were asked before it. Only a test of the rule above can tell.

import torch


def plain_causal_mask(seg, device, dtype=torch.float32):
    n = len(seg)
    causal = torch.tril(torch.ones(n, n, dtype=torch.bool, device=device))
    blocked = torch.finfo(dtype).min
    return torch.zeros(n, n, dtype=dtype, device=device).masked_fill(~causal, blocked)[None, None]


show([0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 2, 2], plain_causal_mask)

   0 0 0 1 1 2 2
0  # . . . . . .
0  # # . . . . .
0  # # # . . . .
1  # # # # . . .
1  # # # # # . .
2  # # # # # # .
2  # # # # # # #

title: The mask
text:
Why it matters
Because of this mask, three questions packed into one request get exactly the answers they would get in three separate requests. That is a property of the mask and not of the weights, so the tests check it on a tiny model with random weights. The other half of the trick is in encode: each question’s positions restart right after the context, so a question looks the same to the model whether it comes first or last. PointerHead then reads the answer off the question’s own tokens, and DecisionModel puts the pieces together.

title: The model
text: babykev is a language model that has been taught to point instead of to speak. Four ideas make that work, and each is one piece of model.py. The reference pages hold the signatures; this page holds the reasons.

title: The model
text:
1. Packing
A request is one context and several questions. encode writes all of it into a single sequence of tokens, in this order: a delimiter and the context, then for each question a delimiter, the instruction, each option between an opening and a closing delimiter, and a decide delimiter where the question ends. The five delimiters are special tokens the base model already has and rarely uses, listed in SPECIAL, so no embedding has to be added or trained: the adapter learns their new meaning.
Text that comes from a caller goes through user_tokens first, which rewrites anything that looks like a special token before tokenizing it. Without that, a context containing the text of the closing delimiter could close an option early. The tests put the delimiters’ text into every field and count the delimiters that come out.
encode returns an Encoded: the ids, and three things the model needs to read them correctly: the segment of each token (0 for the context, k for question k), the position of each token, and where each question’s decide token and option tokens are.

title: The model
text:
2. The mask
The questions share one reading of the context, and nothing else. branch_mask builds the attention mask that makes this true: token i may attend to token j only when j is not after i, and j is in the context or in the same question as i. The mask is added to the attention scores, so a blocked pair gets the most negative number the number type can hold.
Because of this mask, three questions packed into one request get exactly the answers they would get in three separate requests, and the tests check that to the last decimal. The next page shows the mask as a grid.

title: The model
text:
3. Positions restart
Every question’s positions begin right after the context. To the model, a question looks the same wherever it comes in the request, and the tests check that reversing the order of the questions changes nothing.

title: The model
text:
4. Pointing
PointerHead is two small projections. At each question’s decide token it takes the hidden state and projects it; at each option’s closing token it takes the hidden state and projects it; the scaled dot product of the two is the option’s score. One pass gives every question its scores at once. The base model’s vocabulary head is dropped: DecisionModel keeps only the transformer, wraps it in a LoRA adapter when asked, and adds the head. The model has no way to generate text.

title: The model
text:
What trains
With an adapter, the backbone is frozen. Gradients reach the adapter’s matrices and the pointer head and nothing else; trainable_parameters lists exactly those. The smoke run reports how many parameters that is: about 9 million of 503 million.

title: babykev
text: babykev is a small decision model. You send it one document, the context (the state field of a request), and a set of typed questions about it. It returns a probability for every possible answer to every question, in one forward pass. It generates no text.

title: babykev
text:
The contract
A request is a SystemOneRequest: a context and one or more questions, each a Noul, a Choice or a Score. to_record turns the request into the text and the options the model sees, and to_answers turns the model’s probabilities back into answers.

title: babykev
text:
The reference
The pages under Reference are generated from the source, by babykev docs module NAME. Types come from the annotations, the description of each parameter from the comment beside it, and the summary from the docstring. A name in backticks, anywhere on this site, links to its entry: render, choice_confidence, score_confidence. The same text, as plain Markdown, is what babykev docs list and babykev docs module api print at the terminal, for people and for agents.

title: babykev.model

user_tokens
source
user_tokens(tok: PreTrainedTokenizerBase, text: str) -> list[int]
Tokenize a caller’s text so that it can never forge a delimiter.
A tokenizer turns the string <|box_end|> into the special token of that name, wherever the string appears. Text that contained it could close an option early. So <|name|> is rewritten to <¦name¦> before tokenizing, which reads the same to a person and is ordinary text to the tokenizer.

source
branch_mask(seg: list[int], device: str, dtype: dtype = torch.float32) -> Tensor
Build the block-causal mask: a token sees the state and its own question, never a sibling.
Token i may attend to token j when j is not after i, and j is in the state or in the same question as i. The mask is added to the attention scores, so a blocked pair gets the most negative number the type can hold.

title: babykev.smoke
text:
babykev smoke
It loads the base model with a fresh adapter and an untrained pointer head, asks it the questions in the sample data, and prints each answer beside its label. Nothing has been trained yet, so the answers are guesses. What the run shows is that the pieces fit: a line of data passes the contract, is packed into one sequence, goes through the model on whatever device there is, and comes back as answers.
